title: Measuring multidimensional poverty in countries with incomplete data
gist: World Bank researchers present a probability-theory data-fusion method that combines poverty indicators across separate surveys via the chain rule under conditional independence, validated on 571 surveys from 1989-2024; it is 4.5x more accurate in the most common real-world fragmentation pattern than the no-overlap worst case and could extend the Multidimensional Poverty Measure beyond its current two-thirds global coverage, including nowcasts and new dimensions like health and security.

themes.theme: Coverage gap in multidimensional poverty measurement

insights.claim: The World Bank's Multidimensional Poverty Measure can be estimated for only two-thirds of the world in the most recent year even though its individual indicators cover at least 85% of the global population, because the indicators sit in different datasets.
insights.so_what: A third of global poverty measurement is missing for data-plumbing reasons, not data absence — fixable coverage upside.
insights.quote: can be estimated for only two-thirds of the world despite individual indicators covering at least 85% of the global population
insights.locator: Multidimensional poverty measures offer a more complete picture
insights.speaker: @worldbank

insights.claim: Fragmented data adoption of multidimensional poverty measures carries real policy costs, not just technical inconvenience.
insights.so_what: Frames data fragmentation as a resource-allocation problem — better overlap data changes where aid and programs go.
insights.locator: This is because these indicators are scattered
insights.speaker: @worldbank

insights.claim: A new working paper combines poverty indicators from separate datasets at national or subnational level, so that if one survey measures drinking water access and another measures sanitation, the two can be fused to estimate how many people are deprived in both without either indicator appearing in the same dataset.
insights.so_what: Unlocks joint-deprivation estimates from existing surveys — cheaper than fielding new integrated surveys.
insights.quote: if one survey measures access to drinking water and another measures access to sanitation, the two can be combined to estimate the number of people deprived in both — without requiring either indicator to appear in the same dataset
insights.locator: Our recent working paper addresses this data challenge
insights.speaker: @worldbank

insights.claim: The method combines population-aggregated statistics across datasets using the chain rule under an assumption of conditional independence, rather than predicting poverty at the individual or household level.
insights.so_what: Aggregate-level fusion is less data-hungry and therefore scalable globally — a key design choice for replication.
insights.quote: indicators from separate datasets are combined using the chain rule under an assumption of conditional independence
insights.locator: Combining aggregated statistics using probability theory
insights.speaker: @worldbank

insights.claim: Working at the population-aggregate level makes the approach less demanding on data and easier to apply at global scale than household-level poverty prediction methods.
insights.so_what: Explains why this method could actually reach global production use where small-area estimation has not.
insights.quote: it is less demanding on the data and easier to apply at a global scale
insights.locator: Unlike approaches that predict poverty at the individual
insights.speaker: @worldbank

insights.claim: The worked identity is P(p,e,w) = P(p,e) · P(w|e): if drinking water access is conditionally independent of monetary poverty given electricity access, the joint distribution of poverty and electricity from one dataset can be combined with the conditional water distribution from another.
insights.so_what: The exact estimator is transparent and auditable — reproducible by any analyst with two aggregate survey tables.
insights.locator: To illustrate, suppose monetary poverty (p) and access to electricity (e)
insights.speaker: @worldbank

insights.claim: Conditional independence is defended as a reasonable working assumption because poverty dimensions are typically interrelated and driven by common underlying factors, and related research shows benefit in assuming a fixed value for the missing part of the joint distribution.
insights.so_what: The method's central assumption is the main critique surface — where any bias will enter.
insights.quote: In practice, conditional independence is a reasonable assumption, as dimensions of poverty are often interrelated and driven by common underlying factors
insights.locator: In practice, conditional independence is a reasonable assumption
insights.speaker: @worldbank

insights.claim: The method was validated against 571 surveys spanning 1989 to 2024 from the World Bank's Global Monitoring Database, the harmonized collection used to report global poverty, shared prosperity and inequality estimates in PIP and the source for the MPM.
insights.so_what: A 35-year, 571-survey backtest is unusually strong validation for a poverty-estimation method — raises confidence in adoption.
insights.locator: Validating the method with over 500 surveys
insights.speaker: @worldbank

insights.claim: Fusion accuracy scales with indicator overlap: the largest errors occur when no indicators are shared across datasets, and errors decrease substantially as more indicators overlap.
insights.so_what: Gives a practical rule for when fused estimates are trustworthy — check overlap structure before using the number.
insights.quote: As expected, the largest errors occur when no indicators overlap across datasets. Errors decrease substantially as more indicators are shared.
insights.locator: Fusion performs better as more indicators overlap
insights.speaker: @worldbank

insights.claim: The most common missing-data pattern in the Global Monitoring Database, accounting for 32% of cases, has indicators pcews in one dataset and rews in another, and predicting the MPM from it is 4.5 times more accurate on average than the worst case where all six indicators come from separate datasets.
insights.so_what: Real-world data patterns sit near the accurate end of the range, so the method is usable for the plurality of actual cases.
insights.quote: Predicting the MPM from this scenario is 4.5 times more accurate on average than the worst-case scenario
insights.locator: For instance, the most common missing data pattern in the GMD
insights.speaker: @worldbank

insights.claim: The fusion method predicts multidimensional poverty closely regardless of a country's poverty level, not only on average across countries.
insights.so_what: No systematic breakdown in high- or low-poverty tails, which is what would otherwise disqualify it for cross-country comparison.
insights.quote: The method closely predicts multidimensional poverty regardless of a country's poverty level, not just on average.
insights.locator: The method closely predicts multidimensional poverty
insights.speaker: @worldbank

insights.claim: Fusion was tested at national level and at finer population-aggregate levels including rural/urban splits, income quintiles and the lowest representative level in each survey, and additional metrics including an Alkire-Foster application to the MPM were assessed.
insights.so_what: Robustness across aggregation levels means subnational fused estimates are also in scope, which is where targeting decisions are made.
insights.locator: Figure 1 shows the difference between the "true" MPM
insights.speaker: @worldbank

insights.claim: Probability theory allows calculation of the absolute maximum and minimum possible overlaps between deprivations given fragmented data, producing bounds that quantify uncertainty around any fused multidimensional metric.
insights.so_what: Bounded estimates are far more defensible for policy use than point estimates without error characterization.
insights.locator: Probability theory also allows us to calculate
insights.speaker: @worldbank

insights.claim: A simple correction using the median of the theoretical overlap bounds substantially reduces prediction error in fused multidimensional poverty estimates.
insights.so_what: A cheap post-hoc bias correction that materially improves accuracy — the kind of detail that determines whether a method ships.
insights.quote: A simple correction using the median of these bounds substantially reduces prediction error.
insights.speaker: @worldbank

insights.claim: The approach unlocks three applications: estimating multidimensional poverty from surveys missing indicators, incorporating dimensions currently excluded from the MPM such as health or security, and producing estimates for years with no survey including nowcasts for the current year.
insights.so_what: Nowcast capability plus new dimensions would make poverty data timelier and broader — a step change for development data users.
insights.speaker: @worldbank

insights.claim: Knowing not only how many people are poor but how deprivations overlap and where allows governments and development organizations to design more targeted and effective interventions.
insights.so_what: Overlap data changes program targeting, not just reporting — the practical payoff channel for the method.
insights.quote: This is not just a technical achievement: knowing not only how many people are poor, but how deprivations overlap and where, allows governments and development organizations to design more targeted and effective interventions.
insights.speaker: @worldbank

insights.claim: The research was financially supported by the UK Government through the Data and Evidence for Tackling Extreme Poverty (DEEP) Research Program.
insights.so_what: Identifies the donor sustaining global poverty-measurement infrastructure — a funding dependency worth tracking.
insights.locator: The authors gratefully acknowledge financial support
